exclusions.C: The town surveyor, Ida Merrin, found worse than missing slates: rot had eaten into the oak beams, and her report said no repair could make them safe.
exclusions.D: I have stood beneath it on market mornings trying to make out the names, and found myself wishing the old roof could have sheltered the market for one more lifetime.

WV7-P01.5.note: The narrator personally lingers under the kept beam wishing the old hall had lasted another lifetime, a longing for the past rather than amusement, distance, criticism of a rebuild the surveyor showed was necessary, or admiration.

exclusions.A: Nell Ferrin had baked it first, and before she died she made her granddaughter Ada promise to keep it exactly as it was.

exclusions.D: Nell Ferrin had baked it first, and before she died she made her granddaughter Ada promise to keep it exactly as it was.

WV7-P02.4.note: Changing the loaf goes against the promise to keep it exactly as it was, so to break her word is to violate it, not exceed, begin, divide or reveal it.

exclusions.A: Ada had weighed her grandmother's bread against a little trouble, and chosen to sell Tollin a loaf that tasted like any town's.
exclusions.B: So a loaf that had come through sixty years and Nell's own lean winters was given up in an afternoon, to spare Ada a cart and a few pennies.
exclusions.C: Coarse rye could be had in Dunmere all along, and twenty sacks of it sat in Brann's loft.
exclusions.E: Ada had weighed her grandmother's bread against a little trouble, and chosen to sell Tollin a loaf that tasted like any town's.

WV7-P02.5.note: The closing paragraph passes a settled, pointed judgment that Ada gave up a sixty-year loaf for a little trouble when alternatives existed, which is critical rather than detached, amused, hesitantly uneasy, or admiring.
